blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 11 (Special Theory of Relativity), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Why was relativistic mechanics developed at the beginning of the 20th century?
blocks.explanation: New experiments and calculations showed that classical physics based on Newton's laws could not explain phenomena involving extremely small particles or very high velocities. Relativistic mechanics gave a more comprehensive framework.

book_ref.quote: could not explain phenomena involving extremely small particles or very high velocities

blocks.prompt: 2 Why is direction called a relative concept? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Direction depends on the observer. A ball thrown to your right appears to move to the left of a person facing you, so the same motion has different directions for the two observers.

book_ref.quote: This illustrates that direction is a relative concept.

blocks.prompt: 3 Can we say that an object is absolutely at rest? Explain with an example.
blocks.explanation: No. Rest and motion depend on the observer. The walls of a moving train seem stationary to its passengers but appear moving to a person on the ground. All motions are relative to the observer or reference frame.

book_ref.quote: the walls of a moving train seem stationary to passengers inside the train

blocks.prompt: 4 Compare the path of a ball dropped in a train moving with uniform velocity as seen by an observer inside and an observer outside the train.
blocks.explanation: Inside, the ball falls straight down; outside, it follows a projectile path.

book_ref.quote: an observer outside the train will see the ball following a projectile path

rows: Moves with the train at the same velocity vₒ.
Is at rest on the ground.
Sees the ball fall straight down.
Sees the ball follow a projectile path.
Ball lands directly below the point of release.
Ball covers a horizontal distance vₒt before landing.

blocks.prompt: 5 A train moves with a uniform velocity of 25 m s⁻¹. A ball dropped in it reaches the floor in 0.5 s. Find the horizontal distance moved by the ball for an observer on the ground.
blocks.explanation: Horizontal distance = vₒt = 25 × 0.5 = 12.5 m. The observer inside also moves 12.5 m, so for him the ball lands directly below the point of release.

book_ref.quote: It travels a horizontal distance vₒt in time t it takes for the ball to reach the floor.

blocks.prompt: 6 Define a frame of reference and give two examples.
blocks.explanation: A frame of reference is any coordinate system relative to which measurements are taken. Examples: the room for the position of a table; a coordinate system based on distant stars for the position of a spaceship.

book_ref.quote: a frame of reference is any coordinate system relative to which measurements are taken

blocks.prompt: 7 Is a car moving with uniform velocity relative to the Earth an inertial frame? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: Yes. A body in such a car remains at rest unless an unbalanced force acts on it, so the law of inertia holds. Any frame moving with uniform velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial.

book_ref.quote: A body in a car moving with uniform velocity relative to the Earth also remains at rest

blocks.prompt: 8 Why does a car that is suddenly braked stop being an inertial frame?
blocks.explanation: When the car is suddenly stopped or accelerated, a body inside no longer remains at rest even without an unbalanced force on it. The law of inertia fails, so the accelerated car is a non-inertial frame.

book_ref.quote: if the moving car is suddenly stopped or accelerated, the body inside no longer remains at rest

blocks.prompt: 9 The Earth rotates and revolves, yet it is used as an inertial frame. Why?
blocks.explanation: Because of rotation and revolution the Earth is strictly a non-inertial frame, but its acceleration is relatively small, so it is treated as an inertial frame; a body on it stays at rest unless an unbalanced force acts.

book_ref.quote: it is often treated as an inertial frame due to its relatively small acceleration

blocks.prompt: 10 Differentiate between the special and the general theory of relativity.
blocks.explanation: The special theory deals with inertial frames; the general theory with accelerating frames.

book_ref.quote: There is another theory, called the general theory of relativity

rows: Deals with inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference.
Deals with frames accelerating relative to one another.
Covers the effects of speed: time dilation, length contraction, mass variation.
Covers the effect of gravity on space and time, e.g. bending of light by stars.

blocks.prompt: 11 What does the principle of relativity tell us about detecting absolute uniform motion?
blocks.explanation: Since the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, observers in relative uniform motion cannot tell which of them is stationary and which is moving. So there is no way to detect absolute uniform motion.

book_ref.quote: implying that there is no way to detect absolute uniform motion

blocks.prompt: 12 A car moves with speed v and its flashlight is on. Do the driver and a man on the road measure different speeds for the light? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. By the principle of constancy of light, the speed of light in free space has the same value c for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or observer. Both measure c, not c + v.

book_ref.quote: is measured same by two observers, one moving in the car with speed v and other standing on the road

blocks.prompt: 13 Why do space and time become relative in the special theory of relativity?
blocks.explanation: The speed of light c is a universal constant for all observers (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). For c to be the same in frames moving relative to each other, the measured lengths and time intervals must differ, so space and time become relative.

book_ref.quote: Since c is constant, space and time become relative.

blocks.prompt: 14 A person in a train moving at constant velocity close to the speed of light holds a mirror in front of him. Will he see his reflection? Why?
blocks.explanation: Yes. By the principle of relativity no experiment inside the train can detect its constant motion, and light still travels at c relative to him, so the reflection appears as usual. (No material object can actually reach the speed of light.)

book_ref.quote: you will still see your reflection in the mirror

blocks.prompt: 15 What is time dilation? Write its equation.
blocks.explanation: Time dilation is the stretching of a time interval for an observer in relative motion. If tₒ is the proper time, a moving observer measures t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²), which is greater than tₒ.

book_ref.quote: time has dilated or stretched due to the relative motion of the observer

blocks.prompt: 16 Why is the dilated time t always greater than the proper time tₒ?
blocks.explanation: In t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²), v is less than c, so √(1 − v²/c²) is always less than one. Dividing tₒ by a number less than one gives t greater than tₒ.

book_ref.quote: is always less than one, so t is greater than

blocks.prompt: 17 Compare proper time and dilated time.
blocks.explanation: Proper time is measured in the frame of the events; dilated time by an observer moving relative to it.

book_ref.quote: Suppose an observer is stationary in an inertial frame and measures the time interval between two events in this frame.

rows: Measured by an observer at rest in the frame of the events.
Measured by an observer moving relative to the frame of the events.
The longer interval: t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²).

blocks.prompt: 18 A process lasts 4.0 s in its own frame. How long does it last for an observer moving at 0.6 c relative to it?

book_ref.quote: the time measured by the observer will not be

blocks.prompt: 19 Does time dilation apply to living things? Explain.
blocks.explanation: Yes. Time dilation applies to all timing processes, physical, chemical and biological. Even the aging of the human body is slowed by motion at relativistic speeds, as seen by a stationary observer.

book_ref.quote: Even the aging process of the human body is slowed by motion at very high speeds

blocks.prompt: 20 What is length contraction? In which direction does it occur?
blocks.explanation: If you move relative to two points a fixed distance apart, the distance appears shorter than when you are at rest relative to them: ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²). It occurs only along the direction of motion, not perpendicular to it.

book_ref.quote: This effect is known as length contraction.

blocks.prompt: 21 Differentiate between proper length and contracted length.
blocks.explanation: Proper length is measured at rest relative to the object; contracted length by an observer in relative motion.

book_ref.quote: is called the proper length

rows: Measured by an observer at rest relative to the object.
Measured by an observer moving relative to the object with speed v.
Shorter: ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²), along the direction of motion only.

blocks.prompt: 22 A train is 120 m long at rest. Find its length as measured by an observer beside the track when it moves at 0.6 c.

book_ref.quote: If an object and an observer are in relative motion with speed v

blocks.prompt: 23 A metre rod is carried in a spaceship moving at 0.8 c, with the rod perpendicular to the direction of motion. What length does an observer at rest measure? Why?
blocks.explanation: 1 m. Length contraction occurs only along the direction of motion; no contraction is observed perpendicular to it.

book_ref.quote: no such contraction is observed perpendicular to the direction of motion

blocks.prompt: 24 What does the increase in mass at high speed tell us about the inertia of a body?
blocks.explanation: It shows that the inertia of the body increases. As v approaches c, a greater and greater force is needed to change its speed.

book_ref.quote: The increase in mass indicates the increase in inertia that an object has at high speeds.

blocks.prompt: 25 A body of rest mass 3.0 kg moves at 0.8 c. Find its mass.

book_ref.quote: An object whose mass is measured at rest is called its rest mass

blocks.prompt: 26 At what speed does the mass of a body become 1.25 times its rest mass?

book_ref.quote: will have an increased mass m when observed to be moving at speed v

blocks.prompt: 27 Why do we not notice relativistic effects in everyday life?
blocks.explanation: Everyday speeds are extremely small compared with c. Even Earth's orbital speed is only 30 km s⁻¹ against 300,000 km s⁻¹ for light, so Newton's laws hold. The effects become prominent only for particles moving close to c.

book_ref.quote: This is why Newton's laws are valid in everyday situations.

blocks.prompt: 28 What is meant by the relativity of simultaneity?
blocks.explanation: Two events at different places that are simultaneous for one observer are generally not simultaneous for another observer in a frame moving relative to the first. Simultaneity depends on the observer's frame of reference.

book_ref.quote: whether two events are seen as simultaneous depends on the observer's frame of reference

blocks.prompt: 29 In a moving train with light-operated doors, why does an observer outside see the back door open first?
blocks.explanation: Light from the centre travels at the same speed c in both directions. The back door moves towards the light waves while the front door moves away from them, so the light reaches the back door first for the outside observer.

book_ref.quote: This is because the back door is moving towards the light waves

blocks.prompt: 30 You are in a closed frame moving at constant velocity and cannot see any other frame. Can you find out whether you are moving?
blocks.explanation: No. In such a frame there is no way to know whether you are moving or at rest, because the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.

book_ref.quote: there is no way to know if you are moving or at rest

blocks.text: 11.4 The equivalence between mass and energy

blocks.prompt: 31 Write Einstein's mass-energy relation and define rest mass energy.
blocks.explanation: E = mc², where E is the total energy and m the mass, which depends on speed. The energy equivalent of the mass mₒ of an object at rest is its rest mass energy, Eₒ = mₒc².

book_ref.quote: is called its rest mass energy

blocks.prompt: 32 How is kinetic energy expressed in the special theory of relativity?
blocks.explanation: Total energy mc² is greater than the rest mass energy mₒc². The difference is due to motion and is the kinetic energy: K.E. = (m − mₒ)c².

book_ref.quote: is due to the motion, and it represents the kinetic energy of the mass

blocks.prompt: 33 Find the rest mass energy of 2.0 g of matter. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: The total energy E and mass m of an object are related by the expression:

blocks.prompt: 34 A body gains 9.0 × 10¹⁰ J of energy. Find the increase in its mass. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation: Δm = ΔE/c² = 9.0 × 10¹⁰/9 × 10¹⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ kg. The change is tiny even for a large energy.

book_ref.quote: the change in mass m due to change in energy

blocks.prompt: 35 Why does a small change in mass correspond to a very large change in energy?
blocks.explanation: From ΔE = Δm c², the change in mass is multiplied by c² = 9 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻², a very large quantity. So even a small change in mass means a very large change in energy.

book_ref.quote: small changes in mass require very large changes in energy

blocks.prompt: 36 A 2.0 kg body moves at 0.8 c. Find its kinetic energy. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: As mc² is greater than mₒc²

blocks.prompt: 37 A spaceship travels to a star at half the speed of light. Why do its occupants record a shorter journey time than observers on the Earth?
blocks.explanation: From the Earth's view the ship's clocks run slowly, so less time passes on the ship. For the occupants the length of the journey has contracted, so they cover it in less time. Both views give the same result.

book_ref.quote: The occupants of the spaceship record 7 years to reach their destination

blocks.prompt: 38 A spaceship travels to a star at 0.8 c. Observers on the Earth find that the journey takes 20 years. How many years do the occupants record?

book_ref.quote: Let a spaceship be travelling to a star with half of the speed of light.

blocks.prompt: 39 Why is time called the fourth dimension in relativity? Give an example of its use.
blocks.explanation: Time measures the sequence and duration of events and is not absolute, so with the three dimensions of space it is treated as a fourth dimension. Example: a swinging pendulum needs time to give the frequency of its oscillations.

book_ref.quote: In the theory of relativity, time is not absolute; it is considered the fourth dimension.

blocks.prompt: 40 What is space-time, and how do massive bodies affect it?
blocks.explanation: Space-time is a mathematical model that unifies space and time into a single continuum. Massive bodies curve it, like a heavy ball curving a fabric sheet; the more massive the body, the deeper the curve.

book_ref.quote: We can hypothetically visualize this as a fabric sheet.

blocks.prompt: 41 What are geodesics? How do bodies move near a massive object according to Einstein?
blocks.explanation: Geodesics are paths in curved space-time analogous to straight lines in plane geometry. Instead of a force of gravity, bodies and light rays move along geodesics; a body at rest or moving slowly near a massive object follows a geodesic towards it.

book_ref.quote: analogous to straight lines in plane geometry

blocks.prompt: 42 Why is Einstein's theory of gravity considered an advancement over Newton's?
blocks.explanation: Newton gave the inverse square law but offered no explanation for it. Einstein's theory also gives the inverse square law (except in strong fields) and explains why, giving a physical picture of how gravity works.

book_ref.quote: Newton discovered the inverse square law of gravity

blocks.prompt: 43 Which theory describes the bending of light around a star? Why not the special theory?
blocks.explanation: The general theory of relativity. The special theory covers only the effects of speed in inertial frames; the effect of gravity on space and time, such as bending of light by stars, belongs to the general theory.

book_ref.quote: are described by Einstein's general theory of relativity

blocks.prompt: 44 Why does a star seen near the Sun appear shifted from its true position?
blocks.explanation: Light from the star is deflected as it passes close to the Sun on its way to the Earth, so we see the star in an apparent direction shifted by a small angle. Einstein predicted 1.745 seconds of angle, confirmed in the 1919 solar eclipse.

book_ref.quote: We see the star in the apparent direction B, shifted by the angle

blocks.prompt: 45 What are gravitational waves? When were they detected?
blocks.explanation: Gravitational waves are disturbances (squeezes and stretches) in the curvature of space-time produced by some celestial events. They were detected in 2015 and announced in 2016.

book_ref.quote: produced by some celestial events causing disturbances (squeezes and stretches)

blocks.prompt: 46 A pendulum has a period of 2.0 s in its own frame. What period is measured by an observer moving at 0.8 c relative to it?

book_ref.quote: The period of a pendulum is measured to be 3.0 s in the inertial reference frame of the pendulum.
